question: What is the main goal of using a mechanical ventilator in the hospital?

options.C: Eliminate the need for arterial blood gases
options.D: Support breathing while the body heals

explanation: Mechanical ventilation is a temporary support measure that helps maintain oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange until the patient's lungs recover. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h1)

question: In hypercapnic respiratory failure, what problem is the body experiencing?

options.A: Eliminate carbon dioxide effectively from the blood
options.C: Prevent fluid accumulation in the alveolar spaces
options.D: Maintain adequate arterial oxygen saturation levels

explanation: Hypercapnic failure happens when a patient cannot breathe out enough air, causing carbon dioxide to build up in the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h1)

question: Which ventilator setting lets the patient breathe on their own between the machine's regular breaths?
explanation: This mode delivers set breaths while still allowing the patient to take their own breaths in between. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h2)

question: A recovering patient starts every breath on their own and just needs a gentle pressure push from the machine. Which mode works best?
explanation: Pressure support helps patients do the work of breathing themselves by giving an extra push when they take a breath. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h2)

question: What is the main reason for adding PEEP (Positive End-Expiratory Pressure) to a ventilator?

options.A: Reduce the total minute volume requirement of the lungs
options.B: Prevent alveolar collapse at the end of expiration
options.C: Lower the fraction of inspired oxygen to room air
options.D: Increase the peak inspiratory pressure limit safely

explanation: PEEP leaves a small amount of pressure in the lungs at the end of each breath to keep the tiny air sacs from closing up. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h3)

question: Why do modern ventilators often use smaller tidal volumes for patients?

options.A: They prevent overdistention and injury to delicate lung tissue
options.B: They eliminate the requirement for humidified oxygen delivery
options.C: They decrease the need for continuous arterial blood gas monitoring
options.D: They allow patients to tolerate higher levels of carbon dioxide

explanation: Using smaller breath volumes based on the patient's body size protects the lungs from being stretched too far and getting damaged. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h3)

question: What piece of emergency equipment must always be kept right at the bedside of a patient on a ventilator?
explanation: A manual bag-valve-mask must always be ready at hand to manually breathe for the patient if the power fails or the machine acts up. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h4)

question: A patient on a ventilator suddenly becomes restless and the high-pressure alarm starts ringing. What should you check first?

options.A: Silence the alarm permanently to reduce environmental noise
options.B: Auscultate breath sounds and check for tube obstruction
options.C: Administer a large dose of a neuromuscular blocking agent
options.D: Increase the fraction of inspired oxygen concentration immediately

explanation: High-pressure alarms usually mean something is blocking the airway or the tube has moved, so listening to breath sounds helps find the issue fast. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h4)

question: When is the best time to suction the airway of a patient on a ventilator?

options.A: Strictly every two hours regardless of patient clinical status
options.B: Immediately before every scheduled medication administration time
options.C: Only when the high-pressure ventilator alarm sounds continuously
options.D: Based on clinical indicators like secretions or coarse breath sounds

explanation: Suctioning should only be done when you actually see or hear secretions, because doing it too often can hurt the airway lining. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h5)

question: Why is regular mouth care with chlorhexidine so important for ventilated patients?

options.A: It eliminates the need for humidified circuit air
options.B: It reduces bacterial colonization that leads to pneumonia
options.C: It prevents the rubber tube from sticking to oral mucosa
options.D: It stimulates salivary gland function during heavy sedation

explanation: Germs love to gather in the mouth of a ventilated patient; keeping the mouth clean cuts down on bacteria sliding into the lungs to cause pneumonia. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h5)

question: At what angle should the head of the bed be kept to help prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia?
explanation: Keeping the head of the bed elevated stops saliva and stomach contents from trickling down into the lungs. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h6)

question: What complication can happen when a patient breathes very high levels of oxygen for a long time?
explanation: Too much pure oxygen creates harmful molecules that can break down the delicate walls of the air sacs in the lungs. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h6)

question: What is the main goal of a Spontaneous Breathing Trial before taking a patient off the ventilator?

options.A: Verify correct placement of the endotracheal tube
options.B: Determine the maximum peak inspiratory pressure limit
options.C: Assess the patient's ability to breathe without support
options.D: Cleanse the large airways of thick pooled secretions

explanation: This test checks if the patient's body is strong enough to handle breathing on their own before the breathing tube is pulled out. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h7)

question: A patient struggles and gets very tired during a breathing trial. What should the nurse do next?

options.A: Proceed with extubation and administer high-flow oxygen
options.B: Increase the fraction of inspired oxygen and wait another hour
options.C: Remove the artificial airway and insert a nasal cannula
options.D: Return the patient to previous ventilator support settings

explanation: If a patient fails the trial, it means their breathing muscles need more rest, so you put them back on the ventilator support settings. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h7)
